$comment: Corrections applied on top of the reference gir files. 'skip' removes symbols from generation, 'forceOpaque' keeps a record behind a pointer instead of copying it by value, 'rename' overrides the derived C# name, 'annotationOverrides' patches wrong or missing transfer/nullable/array annotations, 'returnTypeOverrides' narrows a returned handle onto the type that declares the member.
$comment-skip-static-str: The *_static_str family stores the string the caller passes by pointer and never copies it, so the string has to outlive every use of the object it was stored in. The generated marshalling hands native code a stack or heap buffer that is released when the call returns, which leaves the library holding a dangling pointer for every string that does not fit the short string optimisation. The gir carries no annotation that says a string must be static, so there is nothing for the planner to key on and the symbols are listed here. Binding them needs hand written glue that hands over an interned copy.
$comment-skip-identity: gst_buffer_remove_meta compares the GstMeta the caller passes by pointer identity against the metas of the buffer. It was listed here because the generated marshalling copied the structure into a local and passed the address of the copy, so the comparison never matched and the call silently removed nothing. That fault is gone: '$comment-force-opaque-meta' below keeps GstMeta behind a pointer, and what the call would now be handed is the address the buffer handed out. What keeps the symbol out is the other end of the same call. Removing a metadata item frees it, and the wrapper the caller passed in is a bare pointer holder that nothing can invalidate, so the object the caller still holds addresses released memory the moment the call returns and every read through it afterwards is a use after free with nothing in the way. A public 'Free' on an opaque record has the same shape and is accepted elsewhere, because it is a call on the wrapper and reads as one at the call site; RemoveMeta(meta) reads as taking an item off a buffer and says nothing about the item being destroyed. Binding it belongs with the rest of the attachment surface, where the wrapper learns to be invalidated.
$comment-skip-annotations: These four functions carry annotations that do not describe what the C function does, and following them produces wrong lengths or wrong ownership: gst_adapter_map returns a pointer whose length is the size argument rather than an annotated array, gst_adapter_take returns freshly allocated memory of the size argument, gst_type_find_peek returns a borrowed pointer of the size argument, and gst_audio_ring_buffer_commit both reads and writes its sample count while its data pointer carries no length at all. An annotation override cannot add a missing array length, so they are skipped.
$comment-skip-consumed: gst_meta_info_register consumes the GstMetaInfo it is given and returns the registered one. The wrapper of an opaque record owns nothing and is never disposed, so nothing is freed twice, but the instance the caller still holds points at released memory the moment the call returns.
$comment-skip-superseded: gst_adapter_unmap releases what gst_adapter_map handed out, and gst_adapter_map is skipped just above. Emitting the release on its own leaves a public Unmap() with no Map() to pair it with, which unmaps a mapping the caller never took and releases a second time the one that the hand written scope holds. The mapping surface of an adapter is Gst.Base.Adapter.Map and the scope it returns, so this entry point is bound there and nowhere else.
$comment-skip-sync-handler: gst_bus_set_sync_handler installs a callback whose return value decides who owns the message: GST_BUS_DROP makes the handler responsible for unreffing it, every other reply leaves that to gst_bus_post. No annotation of the gir states a transfer that a return value turns on, so the generated marshalling cannot express it, and the emitted call had two faults because of it. It refused a null handler, which made the documented clear form unreachable and left a consumer unable to take the handler off at teardown; and its trampoline handed the managed handler a borrowed wrapper, so a handler that answered Drop leaked the reference of the poster with no way of consuming it from managed code. Both are fixed in Gst.Bus.SetSyncHandler and Gst.Bus.ClearSyncHandler, whose hand written trampoline drops that reference itself when the handler answers Drop. Skipping the call also retires the generated GstBusSyncHandler delegate, because the callback emitter only emits what a generated member takes, and the delegate is hand written next to the install so that its documentation can state the contract the binding actually implements.
$comment-skip-deinit: ges_deinit releases everything ges_init built, and the editing services are unusable until another ges_init. The binding runs ges_init from GstGES.Initialize, behind a latch that says it has run, and nothing in the library tells that latch when the resources are gone: a caller who takes the shut down of the process into their own hands leaves the entry point of the module reporting an initialised GES that no longer exists, and no call can bring it back. This is the shape gst_adapter_unmap has, a release with no acquisition of its own to pair with, and the same answer. Deinitialising GES is what ending the process does, which the documentation of the C function says as well.
$comment-skip-unpaired: gst_audio_buffer_unmap and gst_video_frame_unmap release a mapping this binding has no way of taking. gst_audio_buffer_map, gst_video_frame_map and gst_video_frame_map_id all write their result into storage the caller allocates and are rejected for it, so nothing in the surface maps an audio buffer or a video frame at all. That is the shape gst_adapter_unmap has, a release with no acquisition to pair with, and it gets the same answer. Unmap() is the sole public member of Gst.Audio.AudioBuffer, so every call it can receive unmaps a mapping the caller never took; Gst.Video.VideoFrame is the worse of the two, because a frame can be obtained - Gst.Video.VideoAggregatorPad.GetPreparedFrame hands out the frame the aggregator prepared and still owns and unmaps itself - which makes calling Unmap() on it a double unmap by construction. Skipping the two leaves Gst.Audio.AudioBuffer an empty public class, which is accepted for now: mapping either of them needs the hand written scope that Gst.Buffer.Map and Gst.Base.Adapter.Map have, and the release belongs to that scope once it is written.
$comment-skip-credentials: gst_rtsp_auth_credentials_free frees a NULL terminated array of GstRTSPAuthCredential, and the gir spells its parameter as a bare 'GstRTSPAuthCredential**' with no array element on it. The planner reads that as one handle, so the emitted call hands the library the address of a single credential and the loop inside the C function walks past it and frees whatever the words that follow happen to point at. No caller could get it right either: the only producer of such an array is gst_rtsp_message_parse_auth_credentials, whose out array is unannotated in the same way and which is skipped for it, so what a caller can hold is one GstRTSPAuthCredential. That one is a boxed wrapper which frees its own copy when it is disposed, which makes the call a double free on top of the walk. Binding the array needs an annotation the gir does not carry and glue that owns the whole block, and there is nothing to own while the parse call is unbound.
$comment-skip-watch: GstRTSPWatch is an asynchronous RTSP connection driven from a GLib main context, and nothing in the binding can produce one. gst_rtsp_watch_new is introspectable='0', because its funcs parameter is a table of nine callbacks and its notify parameter is a bare GDestroyNotify, so the gir describes no way of calling it and no overlay can bring it back; gst_rtsp_watch_attach takes a GLib.MainContext, which is not bound either. What is emitted is therefore a public class with seven methods, an internal constructor and no producer whatsoever: every one of Reset, SendMessage, SetFlushing, SetSendBacklog, GetSendBacklog, WaitBacklogUsec and Unref is unreachable by construction, and Unref is the same unpaired release that gst_adapter_unmap is. GstRTSPWatchFuncs is the callback table of that call and nothing else; its nine fields are all callback slots, so the record is emitted as a public class with no member at all. Both are skipped rather than shipped as a dead surface a consumer would have to discover is dead. The supported way of driving a connection is Gst.Rtsp.RTSPConnection and its fully bound *Usec calls, which are synchronous and need no main context. Reviving the watch needs a hand written GstRTSPWatchFuncs of unmanaged function pointers and glue that owns the callback state for the lifetime of the watch, and the surface belongs to that glue once it is written.
$comment-skip-cursors: GstByteReader, GstByteWriter, GstBitReader and GstBitWriter are cursors over a block of memory the caller already owns, and that surface is what .NET is built around. The block is a Span<byte>, System.Buffers.Binary.BinaryPrimitives reads and writes every width in either endianness as a single inlined instruction, and System.Buffers.ArrayBufferWriter<byte> is the growing writer, where a bound cursor would cross the P/Invoke boundary once per field. The memory is already reached as a span: Gst.Buffer.Map and Gst.Base.Adapter.Map hand one out and Gst.Buffer.NewMemdup takes one back, and the one search a span cannot express on its own - the masked 32 bit start code scan, which also crosses memory an adapter holds in discontiguous pieces - is bound on Gst.Base.Adapter.MaskedScanUint32. What the bit cursors add over the byte ones is a position measured in bits with fixed width reads and nothing else; no Exp-Golomb reader appears anywhere in the girs, so they answer no codec parsing case either. What is emitted for the four today is why they are listed here rather than left alone: the record emitter drops every method declared on a plain structure, all 148 of them under GstBase in skip-report.md, so what ships is four public value types of raw fields with no member and no producer whatsoever. That is the dead surface GstRtsp.RTSPWatch is skipped for. Listing them also pins the decision, because an emitter that later learns to bind instance methods on a value type would otherwise bind all 148 of them without anyone deciding to. Reversing it is one forceOpaque entry, which is purely additive and can be made at any point in 1.28.x.
$comment-force-opaque-sdp: The payload structures of an SDP message are plain C structures that the library hands out by pointer, and every accessor of theirs takes or returns such a pointer. A plain structure is projected as a value type, which copies it, and the methods declared on it are dropped for exactly that reason, so the media, attribute, origin, connection, bandwidth, time, zone and key surface of the module is unreachable. Keeping the eight of them behind a pointer binds it: the wrapper addresses the storage the message owns, so a read sees the message and a write reaches it. As on every other opaque record, 'Free' and 'Uninit' are public on the wrappers; neither may be called on an instance that a message still owns.
$comment-force-opaque-transport: GstRTSPTransport is the same shape as the SDP payload structures and gets the same answer. It is a plain C structure the library hands out by pointer, gst_rtsp_transport_new allocates one and writes the address into an out parameter, and every accessor takes such a pointer, so projecting it as a value type drops as_text, free, get_media_type, get_manager and get_mime and leaves a structure whose destination and source fields are bare gchar pointers that no caller can read. Keeping it behind a pointer binds that surface and stops the two string fields from being offered as raw addresses. What stays unbound is init and parse, whose transport parameter is caller-allocates='1': a record bound behind a handle is one pointer wide, so the call would write a whole GstRTSPTransport past the end of what it is given, and they move to the CallerAllocates bucket exactly as gst_sdp_media_init and gst_sdp_message_init did. The range structures keep their value projection: GstRTSPRange is embedded by value four times in GstRTSPTransport and GstRTSPTime and GstRTSPTime2 are embedded in GstRTSPTimeRange, so forcing any of them behind a pointer would demote the structures that contain them, and their fields are plain integers that a copy reads correctly.
$comment-force-opaque-meta: A GstMeta lives inside the buffer that carries it. gst_buffer_get_meta and the typed gst_buffer_get_*_meta accessors hand out a pointer into the storage of that buffer, the lifetime of the metadata is the lifetime of the buffer, and a write to one of its fields is meant to reach the copy the buffer holds. A value projection can only ever snapshot it, and all three of the things a metadata item is for are lost by the copy: a read produces a structure that stopped tracking the buffer the moment it was taken, a write reaches a stack temporary that is discarded when the call returns, and the pointer identity that gst_buffer_remove_meta keys on is gone, which also takes with it any chance that what gst_buffer_iterate_meta and gst_buffer_foreach_meta walk over is the metadata of the buffer rather than a copy of it. That third one is not a prediction, it is the fault gst_buffer_remove_meta was skipped for above, which '$comment-skip-identity' records and which these entries cure. GstMeta itself is the header every metadata structure embeds by value as its first field, so the twenty two are forced together: keeping the header behind a pointer while the structures that carry it stay values, or the other way round, is the demotion the range structures of GstRTSPTransport are deliberately left by value to avoid. What the entries buy on their own is the correct foundation - a wrapper that addresses the metadata of the buffer instead of a copy of it - and the methods the gir declares on the records, which a plain structure drops. GstMetaInfo and GstVideoMeta are opaque already and are unaffected. The typed field accessors and the gst_buffer_add_*_meta, iterate and foreach attachment surface are purely additive on top of this shape and arrive later in the series.
$comment-rename-get-type: gst_rtsp_message_get_type reads the message kind out of a GstRTSPMessage, and its derived C# name is GetType, which every object already declares. The generator refuses the collision and skips the member, so the kind of a message would be unreadable; GetMessageType is the name the C# surface gives it. The type of the record itself is registered under gst_rtsp_msg_get_type and is unaffected.
$comment-rename-commited: GESTimeline and GESTrack both emit their commit signal under the name 'commited', with one 't'. The typo is the API, since connecting to 'committed' connects to nothing, so the gir is right and only the C# name is corrected here. The signal name the generated code passes to GObject is the one of the gir; the rename reaches the event alone.
$comment-rename-digits: An enumeration member whose gir name starts with a digit has no legal C# spelling of its own, and the generator used to prepend a bare underscore to it. That underscore carries no meaning, and the names it produced were actively misleading: GST_RTSP_VERSION_1_0 arrived as RTSPVersion._10, which reads as ten and whose value is 16, GST_VIDEO_COLOR_RANGE_16_235 as VideoColorRange._16235, which reads as one number where the C name states two, GST_VIDEO_ORIENTATION_90R as VideoOrientationMethod._90r, and the nine aspect ratio codes of GstVideoAFDValue as _169Letter43Center and its like, where both ratios of the code have run into single numbers. All of them are renamed here so that the C# name states what the C name states. The leading letter or word is the one the underscore stood in for - V for a protocol version, Range for a sample range, Rotate for a rotation, Ratio for an aspect ratio code - and an underscore inside the name separates the two numbers of a ratio, so 16_9 reads as 16:9 exactly as GST_VIDEO_AFD_16_9_TOP_ALIGNED spells it and 16_235 as the [16..235] range its documentation describes. GreaterThan16_9 is renamed for that second half alone: its derived name GreaterThan169 needs no escape and was legal C#, but it sits in the same enumeration as Ratio16_9TopAligned and has to spell its ratio the same way. The generator no longer prepends an underscore for an enumeration member at all: a member whose derived name still starts with a digit fails the run with GEN0016, which names the member and the key to add here, so a gir refresh that introduces one cannot ship a name like this again.
$comment-nullable-callbacks: A callback parameter without a nullable annotation is a value the C contract promises, and the emitted delegate spells it as non-null so that a handler does not have to null check what cannot be null. These four are the places where the gir promises a value the library does not always pass, and each is corrected here rather than by blanket-nullabling every handle a callback receives. The three caps callbacks read their features with gst_caps_get_features_unchecked, which is the accessor that does not materialise them: an entry that carries none hands the callback a NULL, which the gir states for gst_caps_get_features - its return value is nullable - and omits on the callbacks that see the same pointer. GstLogFunction is the prototype of gst_debug_log_default, and every one of gst_debug_log, gst_debug_log_valist, gst_debug_log_literal, gst_debug_log_default and gst_debug_log_get_line annotates its object parameter nullable: logging without an object is what GST_DEBUG does when it is not given one, so most log lines arrive with none. Keys are the c:type of the callback, because a callback carries no c:identifier.
$comment-return-types: The gir spells the factory of a subclass with the return type of its base, so gst_pipeline_new returns a GstElement even though it only ever constructs a GstPipeline. The override narrows the wrapper onto the declaring type, which is the one the C implementation is known to build. The three network clock factories are the same shape with one wrinkle: gst_net_client_clock_new keeps a cache of clocks, which gst_net_client_clock_deinit is documented as clearing, so what it returns is not always freshly built. It is still an instance of the declaring type or of something below it, and the wrapper is created from the real type of the instance rather than from the declared one, so the narrowing holds either way.
